Chapter 3: Confronting Barriers—Fragility, Denial, and Defensive Reactions
As you dive deeper into self-examination, you’ll probably start to notice some internal resistance bubbling up. Sound familiar? It’s actually pretty common.
One of the main ways this resistance shows up is through something called white fragility. That’s when defensive behaviors kick in—like anger, withdrawal, guilt, or feeling the urge to prove you’re “not racist.” It’s all about protecting yourself from discomfort, but here’s the thing: it also tends to shut down the very conversations that could lead to growth.
Denial is another big barrier that pops up. You might hear it as someone saying, “It’s not that bad,” or, “I didn’t mean it that way.” Sometimes, the focus even shifts to things like, “What about reverse racism?” These reactions are understandable—they’re ways of holding onto what feels safe. But, they also keep everything stuck right where it is.
Let’s put this into a real-life scenario. Imagine you tell someone that a comment they made was hurtful. Instead of listening, they get defensive and insist their intentions were good. What happens next? The conversation stops being about the harm caused, and turns into a debate about their character or intentions. It makes real understanding almost impossible.
There are a few other common ways these barriers show up:
First, tone policing. That’s when someone focuses on how a message is delivered, rather than what’s actually being said—maybe dismissing a concern just because it’s shared with strong emotion.
Then there’s color blindness. Claiming not to “see” race might sound well-meaning, but it actually erases the real impact of racism and the lived experiences of people of color.
And finally, performative allyship. That’s when someone takes visible—but pretty shallow—actions to look antiracist, without actually making deeper changes or taking risks.
If any of these sound familiar, you’re not alone. These barriers aren’t unique to any one person; they’re learned responses, designed to keep us comfortable and avoid taking responsibility. But here’s something important: recognizing these patterns is the first big step. It gives you a chance to pause, reflect, and intentionally choose a different way forward.
So, how do you start moving through these barriers? Here are a few practical strategies:
Sit with discomfort. Let yourself feel uneasy without rushing to fix it or explain it away.
Listen deeply. Make it a priority to really hear the experiences and perspectives of people of color—even when it’s tough or uncomfortable.
Take responsibility. Focus on how your actions impact others, not just what you intended. And be open to apologizing and making things right if you’ve caused harm.
This stage is all about building resilience—the ability to stay engaged and present, even when the process feels challenging. It’s about shifting your focus from personal comfort to a true commitment to justice. Because, let’s be honest, real growth usually means moving through a little discomfort along the way.
